headline: NEW CATCH-UP
dek: PRIMARY-SOURCE CLAIM: PGSA said on X that all vessels belonging to the shipping company Sinokor will face 'legal action' starting on Nov 1, because Sinokor vessels committed the highest number of crossing violations in the Strait of Hormuz over the past three months, and 'appropriate actions' had…
sources: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), via its X announcement, reported by Reuters
fault_line: Is Tehran's strait authority a legitimate traffic regulator enforcing rules, or a blockade enforcer using 'violations' to pick off one company's fleet?

sections.what_happened: PRIMARY-SOURCE CLAIM: PGSA said on X that all vessels belonging to the shipping company Sinokor will face 'legal action' starting on Nov 1, because Sinokor vessels committed the highest number of crossing violations in the Strait of Hormuz over the past three months, and 'appropriate actions' had already been taken against at least seven of them. Reuters (via L'Orient Today) and a Devdiscourse syndicated carry report the same announcement; the social sweep independently surfaced the PGSA post itself (Persian text: Sinokor vessels face legal procedures from Nov 1). WHAT 'LEGAL ACTION' MEANS IS NOT SPECIFIED in the retrieved reports -- no seizure, fine, detention or denial procedure is named. Do NOT ship the 'Nov 5, 1405' date seen in one social-post rendering of the PGSA text: the Reuters reports say Nov 1. Related, already recorded: PGSA's non-compliance list held 123 vessels as of Oct 26 (Seatrade, totw-20261026-2300-04).
sections.what_verified: Reuters (T1) reporting the announcement + the PGSA announcement itself (T1 national-official category, STATE (IR)) = 2 families. The announcement's existence is the claim; its enforcement content beyond 'legal action' is unspecified.
sections.what_disputed: No independent confirmation of any Sinokor vessel actually detained, fined or seized under this threat was retrieved; the threat is dated Nov 1, i.e. prospective. PortWatch (stale) shows the strait already near-empty on counted transits, which cuts both ways: enforcement threats land on a thin flow, and a single new detention would be a large proportional event.
sections.why_matters: Hormuz by the Numbers follow-up: Tehran names its next target by company and date -- Sinokor, Nov 1 -- while counted transits (stale Oct 18) sit at 3.7/day against an 85.5/day baseline. Lead with the dated threat, not the backlog.
sections.context: Background: NEW CATCH-UP (Reuters Oct 27, surfaced pre-window ~13:37 via syndication; in no prior scan) -- Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority: all Sinokor vessels face 'legal action' from Nov 1; at least 7 already actioned

totw_analysis: Our read: Hormuz by the Numbers follow-up: Tehran names its next target by company and date -- Sinokor, Nov 1 -- while counted transits (stale Oct 18) sit at 3.7/day against an 85.5/day baseline. Lead with the dated threat, not the backlog. The fault line our audience is arguing over: Is Tehran's strait authority a legitimate traffic regulator enforcing rules, or a blockade enforcer using 'violations' to pick off one company's fleet?
